Hauxwell's thrush (Turdus hauxwelli) attains an ultimate wet body mass of approximately 60 grams [Wwi = approximately 60 grams], a value that places it among the medium-sized members of its genus within the Neotropical avifauna. This asymptotic mass is reached after a period of rapid somatic growth that follows the nestling phase, during which chicks are entirely dependent on biparental provisioning. Newly hatched individuals emerge from the egg at a considerably smaller size, with a recorded wet weight at birth of 6 grams [Wwb = 6 grams]. This roughly tenfold increase in mass from hatching to adulthood is typical of many altricial passerines and reflects the substantial energetic investment required to achieve full structural size. Field observations suggest that the species maintains a steady growth rate during the nestling period, with body mass increments that are closely tied to the frequency of feeding visits by both parents.
